title: Strings
objective: Build and transform text with string methods and concatenation.

sourceAlignment.title: Python Crash Course, 3rd Edition
sourceAlignment.author: Eric Matthes
sourceAlignment.note: Alignment metadata only. Lesson prose and exercises are original Code Forge material.

paragraphs: A string is any text wrapped in quotes. Strings come with built-in methods you call with a dot: name.upper() returns an all-caps copy, name.lower() returns a lowercase copy, and name.title() capitalizes the first letter of each word. None of these change the original string — they return a new one.

You can join strings together with the + operator, called concatenation. Python does not add spaces automatically, so you usually need to include them yourself inside the quotes, and every value you join in must already be a string.

Building a longer message out of several pieces with + gets tedious fast. An f-string solves this: write f"..." and drop any variable — or even a number — directly inside curly braces, like f"Hello, {name}!". Python fills in each {expression} with its value automatically, converting numbers to text for you, so you rarely need + once you're using f-strings.

Text typed by a person often has extra spaces at the start or end. .strip() removes whitespace from both ends of a string, .lstrip() removes it only from the left, and .rstrip() removes it only from the right.
explanation.rule: String methods like .upper(), .lower(), .title(), and .strip() return a new string — they never change the original.

examples.title: Combining and Cleaning Strings
examples.code:
first = "  ember"
last = "forge  "

full = first.strip().title() + " " + last.strip().title()
print(full)
examples.note: Each piece is cleaned and capitalized before being joined with a space in between.

examples.title: Building a Message with an f-string
examples.code:
name = "Ada"
swords = 3
print(f"{name} forged {swords} swords today.")
examples.note: f"..." fills in {name} and {swords} automatically — no + and no str() needed, even though swords is a number.

checks.question: What does name.upper() do to the variable name?
options: Returns a new uppercase string; name itself is unchanged unless reassigned.
Raises an error unless name is already uppercase.

feedback.correct: Correct — string methods return new strings instead of modifying the original.
feedback.incorrect: String methods don't modify the string in place — they hand back a new one.

assignment.title: Forge Banner
assignment.brief: Write forge_banner(smith_name) that prints the smith's name in uppercase, followed by the exact text ' FORGE'.
requirements: Convert smith_name to uppercase using a string method.
Use an f-string to build the final message, ending in the exact text ' FORGE'.
assignment.starterCode:
def forge_banner(smith_name):
    # Uppercase smith_name, then build ' FORGE' onto it with an f-string and print it.
    pass

forge_banner("ada")
assignment.solutionCode:
def forge_banner(smith_name):
    banner = f"{smith_name.upper()} FORGE"
    print(banner)

forge_banner("ada")
assignment.testHarness:
# ---- Code Forge validation ----
import io, contextlib
_cf_buf = io.StringIO()
with contextlib.redirect_stdout(_cf_buf):
    forge_banner("ada")
_cf_result = _cf_buf.getvalue()
print("__CF_TEST_OUTPUT__")
print(repr(_cf_result))

hints: smith_name.upper() gives you an uppercase copy of the name.
An f-string looks like f"{smith_name.upper()} FORGE" — the expression inside {} runs first, then gets dropped into the text.
Store the combined string in a variable, then print that variable.
The final output for 'ada' should read exactly: ADA FORGE
